Of the 101 research records from 2015 onward whose titles name thrust vectoring or vectored thrust,
42 concern fluidic methods, by secondary injection, bypass ducts, dual throats, shock vectoring,
counterflow, coflow or the Coanda effect, as in [Das et al. 2024][research_das_mankodi_2024],
[Kara and Kurtuluş 2024][research_kara_kurtulus_2024] and [Shukla et al. 2026][research_shukla_mitra_2026]. The
diverterless inlet passed from the demonstrator to the production aircraft, whose redesigned three-sided cowl
[retains the diverterless design][ref_codeone], and boundary-layer ingestion into a diverterless intake is measured in [Rein and Koch 2015][research_rein_koch_2015].
**Installed performance accounting, the proper home of the thrust lapse in this article's dash calculation, remains the least glamorous and most consequential part of the subject**,
as installed performance seeking control in [Sun et al. 2015][research_sun_miao_2015] shows. Three clusters
cover this ground, those on nozzles and thrust vectoring, on inlets, intakes and diffusers, and on engines,
thrust and installed performance.

### Performance, Weight and the Programme

**Weight growth is the subject this article's aircraft failed to illuminate, and the literature in this survey treats weight as something to estimate rather than to track.**
No research title in the survey names weight growth. The 26 titles that name weight or mass estimation
treat it as a design method, as in [Nigam et al. 2015][research_nigam_ayyalasomayajula_2015],
[Dababneh and Kipouros 2018][research_dababneh_kipouros_2018] and
[Horvath and Wells 2018][research_horvath_wells_2018]. The production programme met the other side of the question
after the demonstrator had answered every question it was asked, when
[more than 2,700 pounds of unwanted estimated weight had to be removed from the STOVL design in 2004][ref_lm_weight_2004],
and in this survey weight as a programme risk appears only indirectly, through cost growth, as in [Gideon and Wasek 2015][research_gideon_wasek_2015]. They appear
in the clusters on weight, sizing and aircraft design, and on fighter programmes, defence acquisition and cost.

### Acoustics Became a Binding Constraint Somewhere Else

**Noise barely constrained the X-35 and it constrains its successors severely.** The acoustic literature
around vertical lift has grown because community acceptance is now a design driver for civil vertical flight
in a way it never was for a fighter demonstrator at Edwards. The community noise of vertical takeoff personal
air vehicles is predicted in [Kim et al. 2016][research_kim_lim_2016], and the acoustic environment of the
production aircraft's own vertical landings and of short takeoffs from a carrier is measured in
[Reichman et al. 2016][research_reichman_downing_2016] and [Wall et al. 2017][research_wall_mckinley_2017].
The cluster on aircraft, jet and rotor acoustics contains them.

### Method, Uncertainty and Computation

**The methodological change since 2001 is larger than any single technical one.** Uncertainty
quantification, surrogate modelling and machine learning now sit between the wind tunnel and the design, and
a reconstruction of the kind this article performs by hand would today be posed as an inference problem with
stated priors, as the probabilistic flight envelope of an over-actuated aircraft in
[Yin et al. 2019][research_yin_chu_2019], the neural-network system identification of
[Harris et al. 2016][research_harris_arthurs_2016] and the kriging-assisted ducted fan optimization of
[Qing et al. 2019][research_qing_hu_2019] illustrate. **That is better practice and it would not have changed any conclusion here**,
because the quantities that mattered were bracketed rather than estimated. These records sit in the
clusters on flight control, control allocation and handling qualities, and on lift fans, ducted fans and the fan in the wing.

### Powered lift, V/STOL and STOVL aircraft

Powered-lift aircraft of every kind, from the period jet-lift and lift-fan concepts and the Harrier to tiltrotors, tailsitters and the hover and transition of unmanned vertical-takeoff vehicles. **Of these records, 545 were published in 2001 or earlier, and 234 in 2015 or later.**

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

### The Deflationary Reading Can Be Pushed Too Far

**The argument above is capable of proving too much.** If one insists that a demonstration teaching the
engineers nothing new is theatre, then almost every public demonstration in aviation history is theatre,
which is a sign the criterion is wrong rather than a discovery about aviation.

**A demonstration has a second, legitimate function, to establish that separately verified capabilities compose.**
Engineers frequently find that they do not. Doing the three in sequence tests the aircraft's ability to do
them in sequence, including the fuel state, the thermal state, the pilot's workload and the systems'
behaviour after a long, busy sortie.
**None of those is captured by the arithmetic in this article, and all of them are real.**

### Mach 1.05 Is the Worst Place on the Drag Curve, Not the Easiest

**The claim that the supersonic leg was cheap should face its strongest counter-argument.**
Transonic drag rises steeply and peaks a little above Mach one, so Mach 1.05 is close to the most expensive
point on the drag curve, far from a comfortable cruise. An aircraft that reaches Mach 1.05 in level
flight has demonstrated that it can push through the peak, which is a stiffer test than reaching a higher
Mach number would be once past it.

**That counter-argument is correct on drag and does not disturb the thermal conclusion**, which is separate
and which the arithmetic settles. It also does not disturb the ordering conclusion.
**A conclusion that survives its own best counter-argument is worth more than one that needed the argument suppressed.**

### The Assumed Inputs and What They Carry

Several results here depend on quantities that were never published, and the conclusions that would move
with those assumptions should be set out explicitly.

| Assumed quantity | Used for | Does the conclusion depend on it? |
|---|---|---|
| Fan polar moment of inertia, 25 to 50 kg·m² | Clutch energy magnitude | No. The halving identity is exact and the time constant is under a fifth of a second across the bracket |
| Stage loading coefficient of 0.40 | Estimating fan speed | Weakly. Every threshold in the counter-rotation table is an ordinary fan speed regardless |
| Roll-post arm, 2.5 to 4.0 m | Counter-rotation threshold | No. The conclusion is stated across the whole bracket |
| Zero-lift drag 0.025, rolling friction 0.03, nozzle aft until unstick | Ground roll | Slightly. The minimum of 307 to 422 feet stays short of 500 across the weight bracket |
| Rear nozzle at its published 18,000 lbf at eighty knots | The Mission X unstick coefficient | No. The finding is that the record cannot pin a coefficient, and a smaller nozzle thrust only raises the bound of 0.637 |
| Transonic drag coefficient 0.035 | Dash thrust margin | No. The margin is 2.389 and would survive a doubling |
| Sortie fuel burn of 3,500 lb | The floor of the takeoff-weight bracket and the landing weight margin | The gain figure, yes. The finding that the ordering helps does not, since the gain exceeds unity for any positive burn |
| Fan to nozzle separation of 7.5 m | Moment arms and the centre-of-gravity band | Only for the arms in metres. **The station as a fraction, 0.4737, needs no separation at all** |
| Thrust split authority of 10 percent | The pitching-moment threshold | Weakly. It sets the threshold height, and the finding is that the threshold is near a metre rather than far from it |
| Radius of gyration at 0.20 to 0.25 of span | Roll control power | No. The bracket is reported and the residual after a single-rotation reaction is derisory across all of it |
| Oswald efficiency of 0.75, zero-lift drag 0.018, wave drag 0.017 | The dash drag build-up | No. Induced drag is 0.0027 of a total 0.0377, so the build-up is insensitive to it |
| Thrust lapse exponent of 0.7 | Thrust available at altitude | No. The sensitivity is tabulated and the margin survives 0.6 to 1.0 |
| Clutch plate mass of 20 kg | The plate temperature rise | No. It scales the rise linearly and the conclusion is that the bound is absurd, not that the rise is a particular number |
| Clutch engagement time of 9 s | The power bound on clutch dissipation | No. The bound exceeds the dissipation for any engagement longer than about a third of a second |

### A Demonstration Is Not Only an Experiment

**The framing this series uses treats a research aircraft as an instrument for answering a question, and the X-35 does not fit that framing cleanly.**
It was a competitor as much as an instrument. Its purpose included persuading a customer, and a machine
built partly to persuade is not well described by asking only what it measured.
**The framing does not break down so much as become incomplete**, and Mission X sits in the
space that it leaves.

## The Source Base

### Both Halves, Counted and Not Only Divided

**The count and the fraction are reported together, because they move independently and reporting only the fraction misrepresents both.**
Adding contemporary sources leaves the period count untouched while lowering its share, and adding period
sources does the same to the contemporary share. Neither movement is a fact about coverage.

**The research survey holds 4,311 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center.**
Of these, 2,052, or 47.6 percent, were published through 2001, the year the competition was decided,
and 1,996, or 46.3 percent, were published from 2015 onward. Of the contemporary half, 965 records
were published from 2022 onward. **The median publication year of the 4,301 dated records is 2003.**

### The Period Vocabulary for This Article's Derived Subjects

**Several subjects this article's equations name are filed in the period literature under other words.**
The mechanics beneath an equation are not the same literature as the technology above it. This article says
momentum drag, and the period reports say **inlet momentum drag, ram drag, lift engine installation losses
and propulsion-induced effects**. This article says canted joint, and the period says
**swivel duct, deflector, skewed axis coupling and spatial mechanism**. The records cited under those
subjects are filed under the period's words, and the period writes installation effects in the plural, so a
reader looking for them should search in the period's vocabulary rather than the article's.

### A Designation With Almost No Literature of Its Own

**This is the sharpest finding the source base contains.**

**Two research records this article cites carry "X-35" in their titles, and both are papers of 2002.**
They treat the X-35B's flight control law design and flying qualities in
[Walker and Allen 2002][research_walker_allen_2002] and the jet effects test effort in
[Buchholz 2002][research_buchholz_2002]. A paper of the same year, [Roberts 2002][research_roberts_2002], names
the rival's X-32B. No later research title carries either designation.

**The previous two articles found something that looked similar and means the opposite.** The X-33's cluster
held sixty records, of which the X-33 article reports fifty-seven predate 2002. The X-34's held its records and every one predated 2002.
Both programmes were cancelled, and the conclusion drawn was that a cancelled programme stops generating
literature under its own name, so the documentary trace of a vehicle measures how long it survived rather
than what it contributed.

**The X-35 is the control case for that claim and it fails it in an unexpected direction.** This programme
was not cancelled. It won, and its architecture went into production and is flying now.
**And its designation has a smaller documentary trace than either of the cancelled vehicles, because it barely had one.**

What the literature carries instead is the programme name and the product name. Counted by title among the
research records this article cites, 54 name the Joint Strike Fighter in full or as JSF, the dated ones
running from 1996 to 2026. Nineteen name the F-35, the dated ones running from 2003 to
2019, and thirteen of those also name the Joint Strike Fighter.
**Beyond those two papers of 2002, nothing names the aeroplane.**

**The inference this supports is narrower than it first appears, and it is worth stating carefully.** The
X-35 designation was applied to competition demonstrators built by a contractor and flown for a source
selection, and that is not the institutional arrangement that produces published reports. The X-33 and the
X-34 were agency programmes with agency reporting obligations, which is why their cancelled programmes still
left a paper trail.
**So the finding is about who was writing rather than about who won, and the three cases together say that the documentary trace measures the institution rather than the aircraft.**

### What the Record Does Not Contain

There is no published flight test report for the X-35B, and the standard survey of the
[American X-vehicles][ref_xvehicles] treats the type in a page. The two papers of 2002 named above are
the only research records whose titles name the aircraft. There is no published weight statement, no
published engine deck, no published fan map, and no published moment of inertia for the lift fan.
**The quantitative reconstruction in this article is built entirely from performance figures released for publicity and from the physics that connects them**,
and the article says so at every point where an assumption was needed.

### The Definition of Primary

Primary for this subject means the reports and papers written during the competition and the technology work
that preceded it, together with the contemporary programme announcements that record what was flown and
when. **The flight chronology in this article rests on the latter**, because the demonstrator campaign was a
contractor activity and its detailed test reports are not public.

**For counting, primacy is read from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the
NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which
Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. By that rule 651 of the
4,311 research records, or 15.1 percent, are report primaries. **The rule does not reach the
conference papers of the competition period**, such as the inventor's own papers and the two papers of
2002 on the X-35B, so 15.1 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

### Thin Subjects

**Seven subjects are thin in the cited literature, and they are not all thin for the same reason.**
A subject can be thin because the work was never done, because the heading is wrong, or because the
knowledge is so settled that it stopped generating papers, a distinction the X-34 article draws.

The counts are taken over the research records this article cites, so that anyone can repeat them. A record
counts for a subject when its title contains one of the phrases in the second column, matched without regard
to case and with a hyphen read as a space, and a record is modern when it was published in 2015 or later. A
phrase count also catches a title that uses the phrase in another sense, such as an installed thrust reverser under the thrust lapse phrases,
and it misses work filed under another heading, which is what the last column records.

| Subject | Title phrases counted | Records | Which kind of thin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ground roll and takeoff distance | ground roll, takeoff distance, take-off distance, rolling friction | 1, none modern | **Settled.** A closed-form result in every performance textbook, and this article derives it in two lines |
| Disc loading | disc loading, disk loading | 10, one modern | **Settled.** Nine of the ten date from 1948 to 1971, when disc loading was the parameter by which VTOL concepts were compared, and the subject now sits inside momentum theory and lift fan work |
| Jet footprint and ground erosion | ground erosion, surface erosion, deck heating, jet footprint, impingement pressure | 3, one modern | **Wrong heading.** It lives inside impingement and ground environment work, in the cluster on jet impingement, ground effect and hot gas ingestion |
| Rotor spin-up and inertia | spin-up, spin up, spinup, rotational inertia, polar moment, flywheel | 0, none modern | **Wrong heading.** It lives inside drive system transient work |
| Thrust lapse with altitude | thrust lapse, installed thrust, altitude performance | 8, one modern | **Wrong heading.** It lives inside installed performance and engine decks |
| Stagnation temperature and kinetic heating | stagnation temperature, recovery temperature, kinetic heating, aerodynamic heating | 8, two modern | **Moved.** The six older records date from 1949 to 1968 and treat the kinetic heating of aircraft structures, and by title the two modern ones are heating prediction tools for high-speed and supersonic vehicle design rather than studies of the transonic case |
| Standard atmosphere | standard atmosphere, atmospheric model, hydrostatic | 2, one modern | **Settled.** Only one of the two records was published in 2015 or later |

**One homonym is worth naming because it falls on the article's own term of art.**
Figure of merit is a standard quantity in thermoelectrics, where it is written as a dimensionless number,
and in plasmonic and photonic sensing.
**In the contemporary literature, hover efficiency and figure of merit also name properties of solar cells and graphene sensors**,
and the thermoelectric and photonic records are excluded from this survey.

**None of these is padded and none is reported as a gap in the field.** Four of the seven are headings
rather than subjects, and the article cites the literature where it actually lives.
**The three that are genuinely settled rather than misheaded are the ground roll, disc loading and the standard atmosphere**,
and across the three the article cites two records under their phrases published in 2015 or later.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** Much of
this subject's vocabulary also names something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded.
Acquisition also names corporate mergers, biomedical signal recording and seismic surveying. Figure of
merit also names a quantity in thermoelectrics, photonics and power electronics. Ski jump also names dam
spillways and a sport, downwash also names chimney and building plumes, and outwash also names glacial
outwash plains. Engine performance at altitude also names diesel and gasoline engines for road vehicles,
and erosion also names the erosion and corrosion of metals by liquid and slurry jets. Hot gas ingestion also
names the ingress of hot gas through a turbine rim seal, which is a different flow from the reingestion of a
lift jet's exhaust. Harrier also names a bird, swivel also names furniture, textiles and a dictionary headword,
and electric propulsion also names the ion, Hall and plasma thrusters of spacecraft. Impinging jets of water,
liquid fuel, sprays and quenching flows share a word with the jet footprint and none of its subject.
Correction, erratum, retraction and withdrawal notices, figure, table and supplementary-material records,
peer-review reports, conference programmes, news items and journal front matter are excluded as well, because
a survey counts research works and those are parts of works or editorial events rather than works. Reviews of
books, unsigned reference entries, reference entries of two pages or fewer, and the abstracts of papers, patents
and reports reprinted in the abstract sections of other journals are excluded on the same ground, while a signed
encyclopedia article and a textbook chapter are research works and stay.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Underwater vehicle and marine vessel thrust allocation,
planetary gearboxes, counter-rotating pumps and turbines, the kinematics of spatial mechanisms and
manipulators, gas jets impinging on plates and automotive clutches each share the control-allocation,
kinematic, ground-environment or drivetrain problem this article treats. The clutch records are kept in
particular because the drivetrain literature that owns the clutch is largely automotive, but only where they treat
the engagement, its energy or its heat. Electrical machines,
batteries and power electronics written for electric aircraft are excluded, because their subject is the
machine rather than the aircraft, while aircraft-level studies of battery and powertrain sizing are kept. A
reader may weigh the doubtful classes accordingly.

**A record whose only link to this subject is general aeronautics is excluded, and so is one about a vehicle class the argument never uses.**
Hypersonic and combined-cycle propulsion, rockets, launch vehicles and spacecraft, rotor dynamics and
helicopter airworthiness, aircraft systems, maintenance, health monitoring and instrumentation, airline and
airport operations, the noise of transport engines and airframes, transport, supersonic-transport and
high-lift aerodynamics, boundary-layer physics, combustion and emissions, hydrogen storage, railway and
road-vehicle aerodynamics, road-vehicle torque allocation, automotive and marine transmissions, torque converters
and shift control, gear manufacturing and gearbox noise, engine accessories, jet impingement in cooling systems and
heat exchangers, flapping-wing and lighter-than-air craft, and design studies of unrelated configurations therefore
fall outside the survey, as do bibliographies and proceedings volumes. A signed comment on a paper, a discussion of it and its author's closure or reply are research works, because each argues about a result, and are admitted when their subject is, while an unsigned item of these kinds and a referee's report are not. A record on a method or a phenomenon the argument relies on
is kept whatever vehicle it concerns, which is why rocket plumes on soil, ejectors of any working fluid and
boundary layer ingestion on transport aircraft remain.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.**
A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles
only.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

The X-35A [first flew on 24 October 2000][ref_x35] and
[completed its conventional campaign on 22 November 2000][ref_lm_x35c_supersonic]. The X-35C first flew on
16 December 2000 and [completed 73 flights and 58 hours by 11 March 2001][ref_lm_x35c_complete]. The X-35A
was rebuilt as the X-35B, which made its [first vertical takeoff and landing on 23 June 2001][ref_lm_first_vertical]
and [completed testing on 30 July 2001][ref_lm_completion]. On 9 July 2001 it performed its
[first in-flight conversion to hovering mode][ref_lm_conversion], refuelled in the air, and reached an
indicated Mach 1.08 [on the same sortie][ref_lm_shorttakeoff]. On 16 July 2001 it
[flew a short takeoff, a transition and a vertical landing][ref_lm_shorttakeoff]. On 20 July 2001 Major Art
Tomassetti flew Mission X, and on 26 July 2001 Simon Hargreaves repeated it, and on a later flight that day
[landed vertically at a weight over 34,000 pounds][ref_lm_completion]. The
[contract was awarded to Lockheed Martin on 26 October 2001][ref_lm_award]. The lift system's published
figures, which [the LiftSystem reference][ref_liftfan] gives for the production system, are a fifty-inch
two-stage counter-rotating fan producing twenty thousand pounds force from twenty-nine thousand shaft
horsepower, a three-bearing swivel module passing eighteen thousand pounds force and rotating ninety-five
degrees in 2.5 seconds, and roll posts of 1,950 pounds force each. Those figures rest on that single
encyclopaedic reference, and the 2001 company releases give the X-35B only a round total of nearly 40,000
pounds of vertical force. Published empty weights for the X-35B disagree, and none rests on a public
weighing record. The takeoff-weight bracket uses the higher, the 30,697 pounds of the X-35 reference, because
its excess over the X-35A agrees with the [4,000 pounds reported in 1998][ref_tirpak_1998] for the lift fan
installation. The 15,000 pound internal fuel figure matches the operational requirement of that year.

### Engineering Analysis

The fan's figure of merit of 0.697, its induced velocity of 169.3 metres per second, its mass flow of 579.2
pounds per second and its disc loading of 70.2 kilopascals follow from published geometry and performance by
momentum theory. The augmentation ratio of 1.676 and the implied core mass flow of 320.2 pounds per second
follow from the square-root law. The identity that a hovering jet's dynamic pressure equals its disc loading
is exact. The identity that exactly half the energy drawn through a clutch engaging a stationary inertia is
destroyed is exact and independent of the torque profile. The stagnation temperature of 291.2 kelvin at Mach
1.05 and twenty-five thousand feet follows from the standard atmosphere and the energy equation. The unstick
force balance shows that the record cannot pin a wing lift coefficient, since the lift system
vectored to 60 degrees carries all but at most a coefficient of 0.637 at the heaviest weight in the bracket.
The 26 July nozzle deflection is therefore given as a table over weight and coefficient rather than as a
single angle. The minimum ground roll of 307.4 to 421.5 feet follows from the momentum balance with the
nozzle aft, and the 200 foot Mission X roll in the pilot's account is shown to be incompatible with an
eighty-knot unstick at any weight in the bracket. The coefficient of 0.622 to 0.926 at the 180 knot
conversion assumes sea-level density, as the momentum drag does.

The momentum drag of 5,469 pounds force at 180 knots is the fan's mass flow times the true airspeed and is
exact given that flow. The inlet temperature rise of 66.95 kelvin that consumes the hover margin is an
inversion of a corrected-flow relation. The centre-of-gravity station at 47.37 percent of the fan-to-nozzle
distance follows from the hover moment balance and needs no separation in metres. The canted-joint relation
is exact geometry, and the finding that series joints add only when their cants alternate was established by
searching the roll space rather than by derivation. The roll control power of 46.07 degrees per second
squared and the residual 3.083 rest on an estimated moment of inertia and are reported across a bracket.

**Every figure in this section except the series-joint search result can be recomputed from the relations and inputs the article displays**,
and the assumed inputs are listed in the assumptions table with what each
one carries.

### Inference

That Mission X was the assembly of already-demonstrated elements rather than the retirement of technical
risk is an inference from the flight chronology. It is a strong one, because the programme's own
[contemporary statements][ref_lm_shorttakeoff] list every element as already flown four days earlier.
That the novel event was the in-flight conversion of 9 July is an inference of the same kind. That counter-rotation was
necessary rather than merely desirable is an inference from an inverted threshold calculation across a
bracket of assumed roll-post positions. That the short takeoff was optional, a demonstration of
technique, follows from the thrust margin of 1.232 at 34,000 pounds and is close to a deduction at that
weight, but no Mission X takeoff weight is published, and at the ceiling of the bracket, empty weight plus
full internal fuel, the margin is 0.9169 and the deduction fails. Under the lower published empty weight of
23,500 pounds the ceiling margin would be 1.088 and the deduction would hold across the bracket.
**That the conversion was the expensive event is an inference from the momentum drag**, a physical
force of computed magnitude, but the step from a large force to a hard piloting task has not been
measured, since no workload data for these sorties is public.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Whether the fly-off would have gone the other way without Mission X is not settled and cannot be.** Source
selection weighs many things, the flight was [three months before the decision][ref_lm_award], and no public document
apportions the decision among its inputs.

**Whether the X-32 could have flown an equivalent profile with more development time is not settled.** Its
architecture [required reconfiguration as built][ref_x32], but the question of whether that was fundamental or
contingent is a design question that was never taken far enough to answer.

**Several magnitudes are not settled because the quantities they need have never been published.** The
clutch energies need the fan's moment of inertia, the moment arms in metres need the fan-to-nozzle
separation, the roll control power needs the roll moment of inertia, and the pitching moment of the momentum
drag needs the height of the fan inlet above the centre of gravity.
**In every case the article gives the relation that needs none of them beside the number that does**, and
the assumptions table in the framing section shows which conclusions would move.

**Whether the demonstration's persuasive function should count as part of its engineering value is a question of judgement rather than fact**,
and this article deliberately answers it in two directions in two different sections.

## Out of Scope

The production F-35 programme, its cost and schedule history, and the 2004 weight reduction effort are
outside this article, which is about a demonstrator that flew in 2001. The low-observable design of either
competitor is outside it. The avionics and sensor fusion that dominate the production aircraft's reputation
are outside it, because the demonstrators carried none. The carrier variant's approach and arrestment
characteristics are touched on only where they bear on the variant weight argument. The source selection
process itself, and the construct-validity argument about demonstrators generally, are covered in the
article on the X-32 and are not repeated here.

## Conclusion

**The X-35 answered the question of whether a supersonic fighter can hover without being rebuilt between the two, and the answer is yes, by carrying a fan it does not use most of the time.**

The fan is worth carrying because thrust rises as the square root of mass flow at fixed power, so moving air
the engine never touched multiplies vertical thrust by 1.676 without burning more fuel. It is
counter-rotating because a single-rotation fan of that power would have consumed most or all of the
aircraft's roll authority just to hold a hover. Its exhaust is cold because the landing surface and the
inlet both care more about temperature and pressure than about thrust, and the fan presses between half and
three fifths as hard as the core does at a third of the absolute temperature.
**At 34,000 pounds that barrier is worth 66.95 kelvin of tolerable inlet temperature rise before the aircraft can no longer hold itself up.**

**Mission X, the flight the aircraft is remembered for, was not where any of that was established.** Every
element of it had been flown before 20 July 2001, the first in-flight conversion had happened eleven days
earlier on a sortie that went faster, and the arithmetic shows that none of the three events was
individually demanding for an aircraft with 41,900 pounds force of vertical thrust at the 34,000 pounds it is
documented to have weighed on 26 July. No Mission X weight is published, and the short takeoff was flown by
an aeroplane that, on the higher of the published empty weights, could have gone straight up unless it carried
more than about three quarters of its internal fuel. The supersonic dash raised the
stagnation temperature 3.1 kelvin above a standard sea-level day. The vertical landing happened at the
lightest weight of the sortie, in the ordering that makes it easiest at any takeoff weight in the bracket.

**And the expensive event is not among the three.** Engaging the fan at the 180 knots the aircraft converted
at costs 5,469 pounds force of momentum drag, which is 30.4 percent of everything the rear nozzle can
produce, applied above and ahead of the centre of gravity where it pitches as well as decelerates.
**Nothing in the hat trick produces a step change of that size.**

**The sortie was a demonstration in the exact sense of the word, and the label carries no reproach.** It made an
architectural property legible in one flight to people who would never read a test report, and it did so
honestly, because the property was real and the rival did not have it.
**What it was not is the experiment.** The experiment was the clutch engaging in flight on 9 July, and
nobody remembers the date.
## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 84 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 84, 48 are established and 36 are bespoke.
Thrusts and weights are quoted in pounds force and pounds while the relations are evaluated in newtons, kilograms and metres per second, and several letters are reused, so $T$ is a thrust except where a subscript or the standard atmosphere relation makes it a temperature, the thrust is written $F$ in the inlet temperature relations, $L$ is the separation of the fan and the rear nozzle and then the temperature lapse rate, $\ell$ is a roll-post arm and then a bay length, $V$ is the true airspeed except in the fan bay relation, where it is a volume, $A$ is the disc area except in the ground roll, where it is the constant part of the acceleration, $c_p$ is the specific heat of air except in the clutch heating relation, and $r$ in the core flow inversion is the thrust multiplication ratio.

**Equation 1, Thrust and Kinetic Power of a Jet.**
A jet accelerating a mass flow from rest produces a thrust equal to the mass flow times the jet velocity and carries away half the mass flow times the velocity squared as kinetic power.

$$
T = \dot{m} v \qquad \text{and} \qquad P = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{m} v^{2}
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Thrust at Fixed Power.**
Eliminating the jet velocity shows that at a fixed power the thrust rises as the square root of the mass flow.

$$
T = \sqrt{2 P \dot{m}}
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Thrust per Unit Power.**
Dividing the thrust by the kinetic power shows that the thrust obtained from each unit of power is inversely proportional to the jet velocity.

$$
\frac{T}{P} = \frac{\dot{m} v}{\tfrac{1}{2} \dot{m} v^{2}} = \frac{2}{v}
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Disc Area of the Lift Fan.**
The published fifty-inch diameter gives a disc area of 1.2668 square metres.
[Rolls-Royce LiftFan][ref_liftfan]

$$
A = \frac{\pi D^{2}}{4} = \frac{\pi \times 1.27^{2}}{4} = 1.2668 \ \text{m}^{2}
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Momentum Theory Thrust and Induced Velocity.**
Momentum theory gives the thrust of an ideal actuator disc as twice the density times the disc area times the induced velocity squared, which inverts for the induced velocity.
[Momentum theory][ref_momentum]

$$
T = 2 \rho A v_i^{2} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad v_i = \sqrt{\frac{T}{2 \rho A}}
\tag{5}
$$

**Equation 6, Induced Velocity of the Lift Fan.**
The published thrust and disc area at sea-level density give an induced velocity of 169.3 metres per second at the disc.
[Momentum theory][ref_momentum]

$$
v_i = \sqrt{\frac{88{,}964}{2 \times 1.225 \times 1.2668}} = 169.3 \ \text{m/s}
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Mass Flow Through the Fan.**
The density times the disc area times the induced velocity gives a mass flow of 262.7 kilograms per second.

$$
\dot{m} = \rho A v_i = 1.225 \times 1.2668 \times 169.3 = 262.7 \ \text{kg/s}
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Ideal Power of the Disc.**
The ideal power an actuator disc requires is its thrust times the induced velocity, here 15.06 megawatts.

$$
P_{\text{ideal}} = T v_i = 88{,}964 \times 169.3 = 15.06 \ \text{MW}
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Figure of Merit of the Lift Fan.**
The ratio of ideal to published shaft power gives a figure of merit of 0.697.

$$
\mathrm{FM} = \frac{P_{\text{ideal}}}{P_{\text{shaft}}} = \frac{15.06}{21.63} = 0.697
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Total Published Vertical Thrust.**
The fan, the three-bearing swivel module and the two roll posts sum to 41,900 pounds force of vertical thrust.
[Rolls-Royce LiftFan][ref_liftfan]

$$
T_{\text{total}} = 20{,}000 + 18{,}000 + 2 \times 1{,}950 = 41{,}900 \ \text{lbf}
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Multiplication of Vertical Thrust Over the Dry Engine.**
The total vertical thrust over the published dry thrust of the engine gives a factor of 1.676.
[Lockheed Martin X-35][ref_x35]

$$
\frac{41{,}900}{25{,}000} = 1.676
\tag{11}
$$

*Equation 12, Bespoke Thrust Multiplication as a Pure Mass Flow Effect.*
The thrust ratio is written as the square root of the total to core mass flow ratio on the assumption that the whole augmentation is the mass flow effect at unchanged power with ideal jets.

$$
\frac{T_{\text{total}}}{T_{\text{dry}}} = \sqrt{\frac{\dot{m}_{\text{fan}} + \dot{m}_{\text{core}}}{\dot{m}_{\text{core}}}}
\tag{12}
$$

*Equation 13, Bespoke Core Mass Flow Recovered by Inversion.*
Inverting the pure mass flow model with the fan flow from momentum theory recovers an unpublished core flow of 320.2 pounds per second.

$$
\dot{m}_{\text{core}} = \frac{\dot{m}_{\text{fan}}}{r^{2} - 1} = \frac{579.2}{1.676^{2} - 1} = 320.2 \ \text{lb/s}
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Disc Loading of the Fan.**
The published thrust over the disc area gives a disc loading of 70.2 kilopascals.

$$
\frac{T}{A} = \frac{88{,}964}{1.2668} = 70.2 \ \text{kPa}
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Jet Dynamic Pressure Equals the Disc Loading.**
For an ideal actuator disc the dynamic pressure of the fully developed jet is identically the disc loading.

$$
q_{\text{jet}} = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho \left(2 v_i\right)^{2} = 2 \rho v_i^{2} = \frac{T}{A}
\tag{15}
$$

**Equation 16, Exit Density and Area From Continuity.**
For a jet expanded to ambient pressure the ideal gas law gives the exit density and continuity gives the exit area from the mass flow.

$$
\rho_e = \frac{p_0}{R T_e} \qquad \text{and} \qquad A_e = \frac{\dot{m}_{\text{core}}}{\rho_e v_e}
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Footprint Pressure of the Core Jet.**
The rear thrust over the exit area, rewritten through continuity, gives the pressure the core jet applies to the surface below.

$$
\frac{T_r}{A_e} = \frac{T_r \, \rho_e v_e}{\dot{m}_{\text{core}}}
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Isentropic Exit Temperature of the Fan.**
The isentropic relation applied to the fan pressure ratio from momentum theory gives an efflux temperature of 334.9 kelvin.

$$
T_{\text{fan}} = T_0 \, \Pi^{\frac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma}} = 288.15 \times 1.693^{0.2857} = 334.9 \ \text{K}
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Reaction Torque of a Single-Rotation Fan.**
A fan absorbing a shaft power at an angular velocity applies a reaction torque equal to the power over the angular velocity.

$$
Q = \frac{P}{\omega}
\tag{19}
$$

**Equation 20, Roll-Post Couple.**
Two roll posts each producing a force at a distance from the centreline supply a couple of twice the force times the arm.

$$
C = 2 F_{\text{post}} \ell
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Fan Pressure Ratio From the Jet Dynamic Head.**
The ideal disc raises total pressure by the jet dynamic head, which gives a fan pressure ratio of 1.693.

$$
\Pi = \frac{p_0 + q_{\text{jet}}}{p_0} = \frac{101{,}325 + 70{,}229}{101{,}325} = 1.693
\tag{21}
$$

**Equation 22, Isentropic Total Temperature Rise.**
For an isentropic compression the total temperature rise follows from the pressure ratio, here 46.8 kelvin.

$$
\Delta T_0 = T_0 \left(\Pi^{\frac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma}} - 1\right) = 288.15 \times \left(1.693^{0.2857} - 1\right) = 46.8 \ \text{K}
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Specific Work of the Fan.**
The specific work is the specific heat at constant pressure times the total temperature rise.

$$
w = c_p \Delta T_0 = 1004.7 \times 46.8 = 47.0 \ \text{kJ/kg}
\tag{23}
$$

*Equation 24, Bespoke Blade Speed From an Assumed Stage Loading.*
The blade speed follows from the specific work with the work shared equally between two stages and an assumed stage loading coefficient of 0.40.

$$
U = \sqrt{\frac{c_p \Delta T_0}{2 \psi}} = \sqrt{\frac{47{,}002}{2 \times 0.40}} = 242.4 \ \text{m/s}
\tag{24}
$$

*Equation 25, Bespoke Rotational Speed of the Fan.*
The blade speed from the assumed loading coefficient over the fan circumference gives an estimated 3,645 revolutions per minute.

$$
N = \frac{60 U}{\pi D} = \frac{60 \times 242.4}{\pi \times 1.27} = 3{,}645 \ \text{rpm}
\tag{25}
$$

**Equation 26, Work Drawn During a Slipping Clutch Engagement.**
For a source at constant angular velocity driving an inertia from rest, the torque impulse fixes the work drawn at the inertia times the source speed squared.

$$
\int Q \, dt = I \omega_s \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad W_{\text{in}} = \omega_s \int Q \, dt = I \omega_s^{2}
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Kinetic Energy of the Fan.**
The fan ends the engagement holding half its inertia times the source speed squared.

$$
E_{\text{fan}} = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega_s^{2}
\tag{27}
$$

**Equation 28, Energy Destroyed in the Clutch.**
The difference between the work drawn and the energy stored shows that exactly half the energy drawn is dissipated, independent of the torque history.

$$
E_{\text{clutch}} = I \omega_s^{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega_s^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega_s^{2}
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Stored Energy Expressed as a Time.*
The article defines a time scale as the fan's stored kinetic energy over the shaft power, evaluated across a bracket of assumed polar moments of inertia.

$$
\tau = \frac{E_{\text{fan}}}{P_{\text{shaft}}} = \frac{I \omega_s^{2}}{2 P_{\text{shaft}}}
\tag{29}
$$

**Equation 30, Adiabatic Temperature Rise of the Clutch Plates.**
The dissipated energy over the mass and specific heat of the plate pack gives its temperature rise in an adiabatic engagement.

$$
\Delta T_p = \frac{E_{\text{clutch}}}{m_p c_p} = \frac{I \omega_s^{2}}{2 m_p c_p}
\tag{30}
$$

*Equation 31, Bespoke Upper Bound on Clutch Dissipation.*
At most half the rated shaft power can be destroyed over an engagement time the article assumes to be nine seconds, which bounds the dissipation at 97.3 megajoules.

$$
E_{\text{clutch}} \le \tfrac{1}{2} P t = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 21.63 \times 10^{6} \times 9 = 97.3 \ \text{MJ}
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Dissipation as a Share of the Bound.*
The bracketed dissipation for the assumed inertias, spread over the assumed nine seconds, is between 1.9 and 3.7 percent of the bound.

$$
\frac{E_{\text{clutch}} / t}{\tfrac{1}{2} P} = \frac{E_{\text{clutch}}}{\tfrac{1}{2} P t} = \frac{1.82}{97.3} = 0.0187 \quad \text{to} \quad \frac{3.64}{97.3} = 0.0374
\tag{32}
$$

**Equation 33, Momentum Drag of the Lift Fan.**
A fan ingesting air at the flight speed and discharging it vertically suffers a drag equal to its mass flow times the true airspeed.

$$
D_{\text{mom}} = \dot{m} V
\tag{33}
$$

*Equation 34, Bespoke Deceleration From Momentum Drag at Conversion.*
The momentum drag at 180 knots is computed with the sea-level fan mass flow, an assumption at the conversion altitude, and divided by a mass of 34,000 pounds.
[eleven days earlier][ref_lm_conversion]

$$
a = \frac{D_{\text{mom}}}{m} = \frac{24{,}329}{15{,}422} = 1.578 \ \text{m/s}^{2} = 0.1609 \, g
\tag{34}
$$

*Equation 35, Bespoke Available Pitch Moment.*
The pitch moment available is taken as an assumed ten percent of the fan thrust acting on a moment arm that rests on an assumed fan to nozzle separation of 7.5 metres.
[Rolls-Royce LiftFan][ref_liftfan]

$$
M_{\text{avail}} = 0.10 \, T_f x_f = 0.10 \times 88{,}964 \times 3.553 = 31{,}606 \ \text{N m}
\tag{35}
$$

*Equation 36, Bespoke Inlet Height at Which Momentum Drag Exhausts Pitch Authority.*
The assumed pitch moment over the momentum drag gives the inlet height of 1.299 metres at which the two are equal.

$$
h^{*} = \frac{M_{\text{avail}}}{D_{\text{mom}}} = \frac{31{,}606}{24{,}329} = 1.299 \ \text{m}
\tag{36}
$$

**Equation 37, Hover Moment Balance.**
In steady hover the moment of the fan thrust about the centre of gravity cancels that of the rear nozzle.

$$
T_f x_f = T_r x_r
\tag{37}
$$

**Equation 38, Centre of Gravity Fixed by the Hover Balance.**
The moment balance with the published fan and rear nozzle thrusts places the centre of gravity at 47.37 percent of the separation behind the fan.

$$
\frac{x_f}{L} = \frac{T_r}{T_f + T_r} = \frac{18{,}000}{38{,}000} = 0.4737
\tag{38}
$$

*Equation 39, Bespoke Thrust Lapse With Inlet Temperature.*
The thrust is taken to fall as the inverse of inlet total temperature, a simplification the article adopts for a fixed corrected operating point.

$$
\frac{F}{F_{0}} = \frac{T_{\text{amb}}}{T_{\text{amb}} + \Delta T}
\tag{39}
$$

*Equation 40, Bespoke Critical Inlet Temperature Rise.*
Inverting the assumed thrust lapse at a weight of 34,000 pounds gives the inlet temperature rise of 66.95 kelvin that consumes the hover margin.

$$
\Delta T_{\text{crit}} = T_{\text{amb}} \left(\frac{F_{\text{total}}}{W} - 1\right) = 288.15 \times 0.2324 = 66.95 \ \text{K}
\tag{40}
$$

**Equation 41, Mean Slew Rate of the Swivel Module.**
The published sweep of ninety-five degrees in 2.5 seconds is a mean slew rate of 38.0 degrees per second.
[Rolls-Royce LiftFan][ref_liftfan]

$$
\dot{\delta} = \frac{\Delta \delta}{\Delta t} = \frac{95^{\circ}}{2.5 \ \text{s}} = 38.0 \ \text{deg/s}
\tag{41}
$$

**Equation 42, Deflection of a Single Canted Joint.**
Rolling one side of a joint canted at an angle to the duct axis deflects the downstream axis by an amount that reaches twice the cant at half a turn.

$$
\cos\delta = \cos^{2}\beta + \sin^{2}\beta \cos\phi
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Cant Required of a Single Bearing.**
A single joint must be canted at half the required ninety-five degree deflection, or 47.5 degrees.

$$
\beta_{\text{single}} = \frac{95^{\circ}}{2} = 47.5^{\circ}
\tag{43}
$$

*Equation 44, Bespoke Cant Required of Three Alternating Bearings.*
Taking three alternating joints to reach six times their common cant, a result of the article's own numerical search, the required cant is 15.83 degrees.

$$
\beta_{\text{three}} = \frac{95^{\circ}}{6} = 15.83^{\circ}
\tag{44}
$$

**Equation 45, Roll Acceleration From the Roll Posts.**
The roll angular acceleration is the roll-post couple divided by the roll moment of inertia.

$$
\dot{p} = \frac{2 F_{\text{post}} \ell}{I_{xx}}
\tag{45}
$$

*Equation 46, Bespoke Roll Moment of Inertia.*
The roll inertia is estimated with a radius of gyration the article assumes to be 0.22 of the span.

$$
I_{xx} = m k_x^{2} = 15{,}422 \times 2.213^{2} = 75{,}400 \ \text{kg m}^{2}
\tag{46}
$$

*Equation 47, Bespoke Roll Acceleration With the Posts at 3.5 Metres.*
The roll acceleration uses the assumed roll inertia and an assumed roll-post arm of 3.5 metres.

$$
\dot{p} = \frac{60{,}718}{75{,}400} = 0.805 \ \text{rad/s}^{2} = 46.07 \ \text{deg/s}^{2}
\tag{47}
$$

*Equation 48, Bespoke Residual Roll Acceleration With a Single-Rotation Fan.*
The roll acceleration left after a single-rotation fan's reaction torque at the estimated speed is about three degrees per second squared.

$$
\dot{p}_{\text{residual}} = \frac{4{,}063}{75{,}400} = 3.083 \ \text{deg/s}^{2}
\tag{48}
$$

**Equation 49, Swept Volume of the Fan.**
The fan bay is at least the swept volume of the fan, its disc area times the bay length.

$$
V = \frac{\pi D^{2}}{4} \ell
\tag{49}
$$

*Equation 50, Bespoke Fuel Displaced by the Fan Bay.*
The fuel weight lost to the fan uses a bay length near the middle of an assumed range of 1.2 to 1.6 metres and an assumed fuel density of 800 kilograms per cubic metre.

$$
W_{\text{fuel}} = \rho_f V = 800 \times 1.773 = 1{,}419 \ \text{kg} = 3{,}128 \ \text{lb}
\tag{50}
$$

**Equation 51, Unstick Condition and Lift Equation.**
An aircraft leaves the ground once wing lift and downward lift system thrust together reach the weight, with lift given by the standard lift equation.

$$
L + T_v \ge W, \qquad L = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} S C_L
\tag{51}
$$

**Equation 52, Thrust That Points Down Whatever the Nozzle Does.**
The published fan thrust and the two roll posts sum to 23,900 pounds force.

$$
T_f = 20{,}000 + 2 \times 1{,}950 = 23{,}900 \ \text{lbf}
\tag{52}
$$

*Equation 53, Bespoke Vectored Lift at the Mission X Unstick.*
The vertical thrust assumes that the rear nozzle delivers its published 18,000 pounds force at eighty knots when vectored to 60 degrees.

$$
T_v = T_f + T_r \sin\theta = 23{,}900 + 18{,}000 \sin 60^{\circ} = 23{,}900 + 15{,}588 = 39{,}488 \ \text{lbf}
\tag{53}
$$

**Equation 54, Dynamic Pressure Times Wing Area at Eighty Knots.**
At eighty knots and sea-level density over the wing area the product of dynamic pressure and area is 9,751 pounds force.

$$
\tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} S = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.225 \times 41.156^{2} \times 41.81 = 43{,}376 \ \text{N} = 9{,}751 \ \text{lbf}
\tag{54}
$$

*Equation 55, Bespoke Upper Bound on the Unstick Lift Coefficient.*
The lift coefficient required at the ceiling of the article's weight bracket, with the assumed vectored thrust, is at most 0.637.

$$
C_L \ge \frac{W - T_v}{\tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} S} = \frac{45{,}697 - 39{,}488}{9{,}751} = 0.637
\tag{55}
$$

**Equation 56, Dynamic Pressure Times Wing Area at Sixty Knots.**
At sixty knots and sea-level density the product of dynamic pressure and wing area is 5,485 pounds force.

$$
\tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} S = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.225 \times 30.867^{2} \times 41.81 = 24{,}399 \ \text{N} = 5{,}485 \ \text{lbf}
\tag{56}
$$

**Equation 57, Nozzle Deflection That Balances the Weight.**
Solving the unstick condition for the nozzle deflection gives its sine in terms of the weight, the downward thrust, the wing lift and the rear thrust.

$$
\sin\theta = \frac{W - T_f - C_L \, \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} S}{T_r}
\tag{57}
$$

*Equation 58, Bespoke Lift Coefficient at the First Conversion.*
The lift coefficient at the 180 knot conversion is evaluated at sea-level density, which the article states as an assumption at 9,000 feet.
[eleven days earlier][ref_lm_conversion]

$$
C_L = \frac{W}{\tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} S}, \qquad \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.225 \times 92.6^{2} \times 41.81 = 219{,}588 \ \text{N} = 49{,}365 \ \text{lbf}
\tag{58}
$$

*Equation 59, Bespoke Lift Coefficient Range at Conversion.*
Across a weight bracket from the empty weight taken for it to full internal fuel, the sea-level coefficient runs from 0.622 to 0.926.

$$
C_L = \frac{30{,}697}{49{,}365} = 0.622 \quad \text{to} \quad \frac{45{,}697}{49{,}365} = 0.926
\tag{59}
$$

**Equation 60, Mean Acceleration for the Quoted Mission X Roll.**
Reaching eighty knots from rest in the quoted 200 feet requires a mean acceleration of 1.417 times standard gravity.

$$
\bar{a} = \frac{V^{2}}{2 s} = \frac{41.156^{2}}{2 \times 60.96} = 13.89 \ \text{m/s}^{2} = 1.417 \, g
\tag{60}
$$

*Equation 61, Bespoke Maximum Acceleration With All Thrust Aft.*
Pointing all published thrust aft with no drag or friction at the bracket floor of 34,197 pounds, which rests on an assumed fuel burn, allows at most 1.225 times standard gravity.

$$
\frac{a_{\max}}{g} = \frac{T_{\text{total}}}{W} = \frac{41{,}900}{34{,}197} = 1.225
\tag{61}
$$

*Equation 62, Bespoke Frictionless Minimum Ground Roll.*
Only the rear nozzle thrust at the bracket floor weight, with no drag or rolling friction, gives a minimum roll of 538.3 feet.

$$
s_{\min} = \frac{V^{2}}{2 g \, T_r / W} = \frac{41.156^{2}}{2 \times 9.80665 \times 0.5264} = 164.1 \ \text{m} = 538.3 \ \text{ft}
\tag{62}
$$

*Equation 63, Bespoke Ground Roll Equation of Motion.*
The equation of motion takes the rear nozzle as pointing aft until unstick, an assumption for the 26 July flight, with rolling friction and zero-lift drag.

$$
m \frac{dV}{dt} = T_r \cos\theta - \mu \left(W - T_v\right) - \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} S C_{D_0}, \qquad \theta = 0
\tag{63}
$$

**Equation 64, Closed-Form Distance Under Constant and Quadratic Deceleration.**
Integrating an acceleration made of a constant part less a term in the square of speed gives the distance in closed form.

$$
s = \frac{1}{2B} \ln\!\left(\frac{A}{A - B V^{2}}\right)
\tag{64}
$$

*Equation 65, Bespoke Minimum Roll on 26 July.*
The closed form evaluated with the constants built from the assumed friction and drag at 34,000 pounds gives a minimum roll of 307.4 feet.

$$
s_{\min} = 93.69 \ \text{m} = 307.4 \ \text{ft}
\tag{65}
$$

**Equation 66, Mean Acceleration for the Quoted 26 July Roll.**
The quoted roll of about five hundred feet to sixty knots requires a mean acceleration of 0.3187 times standard gravity.

$$
\bar{a} = \frac{V^{2}}{2 s_q} = \frac{30.867^{2}}{2 \times 152.4} = 3.126 \ \text{m/s}^{2} = 0.3187 \, g
\tag{66}
$$

*Equation 67, Bespoke Acceleration Available During the Roll.*
The acceleration available is approximated by the constant part less the drag term evaluated at half the squared unstick speed.

$$
a_{\text{avail}} = A - \tfrac{1}{2} B V^{2}
\tag{67}
$$

**Equation 68, Largest Weight the Lift System Can Hold.**
The total vertical thrust over standard gravity gives a largest supportable weight of 41,900 pounds.

$$
W_{\max} = \frac{T_{\text{total}}}{g} = \frac{186{,}381}{9.80665} = 19{,}006 \ \text{kg} = 41{,}900 \ \text{lb}
\tag{68}
$$

**Equation 69, Hover Margin at the Documented Weight.**
The total vertical thrust over the documented 34,000 pounds gives a margin of 1.232.
[flown to about Mach 1.2][ref_lm_completion]

$$
\frac{T_{\text{total}}}{W} = \frac{41{,}900}{34{,}000} = 1.232
\tag{69}
$$

*Equation 70, Bespoke Mission X Takeoff Weight Bracket.*
The takeoff weight is bracketed between the empty weight plus an assumed burn of 3,500 pounds and the empty weight plus full internal fuel, neglecting the pilot and instrumentation.
[Lockheed Martin X-35][ref_x35]

$$
W_{\text{TO}} = W_{\text{empty}} + W_{\text{fuel}}, \qquad 30{,}697 + 3{,}500 = 34{,}197 \ \le \ W_{\text{TO}} \ \le \ 30{,}697 + 15{,}000 = 45{,}697 \ \text{lb}
\tag{70}
$$

*Equation 71, Bespoke Hover Margin at the Ceiling of the Bracket.*
At the ceiling of the article's bracket the margin falls to 0.9169, so vertical takeoff at full internal fuel was impossible.

$$
\frac{T_{\text{total}}}{W_{\text{TO}}} = \frac{41{,}900}{45{,}697} = 0.9169
\tag{71}
$$

**Equation 72, Temperature and Pressure in the Standard Troposphere.**
Below the tropopause the temperature falls linearly with altitude and the hydrostatic equation integrates to a power law in pressure.

$$
T = T_{\text{SL}} - Lh \qquad \text{and} \qquad p = p_{\text{SL}} \left(\frac{T}{T_{\text{SL}}}\right)^{\frac{g_0}{RL}}
\tag{72}
$$

**Equation 73, Exponent of the Tropospheric Pressure Law.**
Standard gravity over the gas constant and the lapse rate gives an exponent of 5.2559.

$$
\frac{g_0}{RL} = \frac{9.80665}{287.05 \times 0.0065} = 5.2559
\tag{73}
$$

**Equation 74, Density and Speed of Sound at Twenty-Five Thousand Feet.**
The ideal gas law and the speed of sound relation give the density and speed of sound at 7,620 metres in the standard atmosphere.

$$
\rho = \frac{p}{RT} = 0.5489 \ \text{kg/m}^{3} \qquad \text{and} \qquad a = \sqrt{\gamma R T} = 309.7 \ \text{m/s}
\tag{74}
$$

**Equation 75, Stagnation Temperature of the Supersonic Dash.**
The energy equation gives a stagnation temperature of 291.2 kelvin at Mach 1.05 and twenty-five thousand feet.

$$
T_0 = T + \frac{V^{2}}{2 c_p} = 238.62 + \frac{325.2^{2}}{2 \times 1004.7} = 291.2 \ \text{K}
\tag{75}
$$

**Equation 76, Dynamic Pressure of the Dash.**
Half the standard density times the speed squared gives 29,018 pascals at Mach 1.05.

$$
q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5489 \times 325.2^{2} = 29{,}018 \ \text{Pa}
\tag{76}
$$

*Equation 77, Bespoke Lift Coefficient of the Dash.*
The lift coefficient takes the dash weight as 34,000 pounds, the figure documented for a different flight.

$$
C_L = \frac{W}{qS} = \frac{151{,}240}{29{,}018 \times 41.81} = 0.1247
\tag{77}
$$

*Equation 78, Bespoke Induced Drag Coefficient of the Dash.*
The induced drag coefficient uses an Oswald efficiency the article assumes to be 0.75.

$$
C_{D_i} = \frac{C_L^{2}}{\pi \, \mathrm{AR} \, e} = \frac{0.1247^{2}}{\pi \times 2.42 \times 0.75} = 0.002726
\tag{78}
$$

*Equation 79, Bespoke Drag Build-Up of the Dash.*
The drag coefficient adds an assumed zero-lift coefficient of 0.018 and an assumed wave-drag increment of 0.017 to the induced term.

$$
C_D = C_{D_0} + C_{D_w} + C_{D_i} = 0.018 + 0.017 + 0.002726 = 0.03773
\tag{79}
$$

*Equation 80, Bespoke Drag of the Dash.*
The dynamic pressure times the wing area times the assumed drag build-up gives a drag of 10,289 pounds force.

$$
D = q S C_D = 29{,}018 \times 41.81 \times 0.03773 = 45{,}771 \ \text{N} = 10{,}289 \ \text{lbf}
\tag{80}
$$

*Equation 81, Bespoke Thrust Available at Altitude.*
The thrust available is a sea-level thrust of 40,000 pounds force times the density ratio raised to an exponent the article assumes to be 0.7.

$$
T = T_{\text{SL}} \sigma^{n} = 40{,}000 \times 0.4481^{0.7} = 40{,}000 \times 0.5701 = 22{,}805 \ \text{lbf}
\tag{81}
$$

*Equation 82, Bespoke Thrust to Drag Margin of the Dash.*
The assumed thrust lapse against the assumed drag build-up gives a thrust to drag ratio of 2.216.

$$
\frac{T}{D} = \frac{22{,}805}{10{,}289} = 2.216 \qquad \text{or} \qquad \frac{D}{T} = \frac{10{,}289}{22{,}805} = 0.451
\tag{82}
$$

*Equation 83, Bespoke Gain in Hover Margin From Landing Last.*
The article defines the gain from the ordering as the ratio of landing to takeoff margin, which reduces to the takeoff weight over the takeoff weight less the assumed fuel burn.

$$
\frac{T_{\text{total}} / W_{\text{land}}}{T_{\text{total}} / W_{\text{TO}}} = \frac{W_{\text{TO}}}{W_{\text{TO}} - W_{\text{fuel}}}
\tag{83}
$$

*Equation 84, Bespoke Landing Margin at the Ceiling With a Hot Inlet.*
At the ceiling landing weight the margin is reduced by the assumed thrust lapse for a ten kelvin inlet temperature rise to 0.960.

$$
\frac{T_{\text{total}}}{W_{\text{land}}} \cdot \frac{T_{\text{amb}}}{T_{\text{amb}} + \Delta T} = \frac{41{,}900}{42{,}197} \times \frac{288.15}{298.15} = 0.960
\tag{84}
$$

### Notation

- $\dot{m}$, the mass flow, with $\dot{m}_{\text{fan}}$ the fan flow and $\dot{m}_{\text{core}}$ the engine core flow
- $v_i$, the induced velocity at the disc
- $P_{\text{shaft}}$, the shaft power absorbed by the fan, with $P_{\text{ideal}}$ the ideal power of the disc
- $\mathrm{FM}$, the figure of merit of the fan
- $T_{\text{total}}$, the total vertical thrust of the lift system, with $T_{\text{dry}}$ the dry thrust of the engine
- $T_f$, the thrust of the lift fan, with $T_r$ the thrust of the rear nozzle and $T_v$ the downward thrust of the lift system
- $x_f$, the distance of the fan behind or ahead of the centre of gravity, with $x_r$ that of the rear nozzle
- $q_{\text{jet}}$, the dynamic pressure of the fully developed jet
- $\Pi$, the fan pressure ratio
- $\psi$, the stage loading coefficient
- $U$, the blade speed
- $Q$, the torque
- $F_{\text{post}}$, the thrust of one roll post
- $\ell$, the roll-post arm, and in the fan bay relation the bay length
- $\omega_s$, the angular velocity of the driving source
- $I_{xx}$, the roll moment of inertia, with $k_x$ the radius of gyration in roll
- $E_{\text{clutch}}$, the energy dissipated in the clutch, with $E_{\text{fan}}$ the kinetic energy of the fan
- $\tau$, the stored energy of the fan expressed as a time
- $D_{\text{mom}}$, the momentum drag of the lift fan
- $M_{\text{avail}}$, the pitch moment available, with $h^{*}$ the inlet height at which it equals the momentum drag moment
- $\Delta T_0$, the total temperature rise across the fan, with $\Delta T$ an inlet temperature rise
- $T_{\text{amb}}$, the ambient temperature
- $\delta$, the deflection of the duct axis
- $\beta$, the cant angle of a joint
- $\phi$, the relative roll angle of the two sides of a joint
- $\dot{p}$, the roll angular acceleration
- $W_{\text{TO}}$, the takeoff weight, with $W_{\text{land}}$ the landing weight and $W_{\text{empty}}$ the empty weight
- $W_{\text{fuel}}$, the fuel weight
- $\theta$, the deflection of the rear nozzle below the horizontal
- $\mu$, the rolling friction coefficient
- $C_{D_0}$, the zero-lift drag coefficient, with $C_{D_w}$ the wave-drag increment and $C_{D_i}$ the induced drag coefficient
- $\mathrm{AR}$, the wing aspect ratio
- $\sigma$, the density ratio against sea level
- $T_{\text{SL}}$, a sea-level value, the sea-level temperature in the atmosphere relation and the sea-level thrust in the thrust lapse
